parts.title: 7-Day Topic Progression Plan
parts.body:
# 7-Day Linear Algebra Basics — Structured Outline

## Day 1 — Vectors in ℝ² and ℝ³
**Main topic:** Vector arithmetic and geometric meaning in low dimensions.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Vector addition & scalar multiplication | Component-wise rules; geometric (tip-to-tail) picture |
| 2 | Dot product (inner product) | Formula, orthogonality test, projection of one vector onto another |
| 3 | Cross product (ℝ³ only) | Right-hand rule, magnitude = parallelogram area, orthogonality to both inputs |
| 4 | Length, angle, unit vectors | ‖v‖ = √(v·v); cos θ = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖); normalisation |

**Why here:** Vectors are the atoms of linear algebra. Every later object (matrix, subspace, solution set) is built from vectors and the operations defined on them. Starting in ℝ²/ℝ³ gives a concrete geometric anchor before abstracting.

---

## Day 2 — Vector Spaces, Span, and Linear Independence
**Main topic:** The structure that vectors live in.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Span & linear combinations | What set of vectors does {v₁,…,vₖ} "cover"? |
| 2 | Linear independence / dependence | Definition via c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ=0; geometric intuition (collinear, coplanar) |
| 3 | Basis & dimension | Minimal spanning set; dim(ℝⁿ)=n; non-uniqueness of bases |
| 4 | Subspaces of ℝⁿ | Row space, column space, null space (introduction — full treatment in Day 6) |

**Why here:** Before manipulating matrices you need to know *what space they act on* and whether a set of vectors is redundant. Independence/dimension reasoning is the language for rank and solution uniqueness that appear in Days 4–5.

---

## Day 3 — Matrices & Matrix Operations
**Main topic:** Matrices as compact representations of linear maps.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Matrix addition, scalar multiplication, transpose | Entry-wise rules; (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ |
| 2 | Matrix multiplication (row-column) | Dimensions must match; composition of linear maps; **non-commutativity** |
| 3 | Inverse matrices | A⁻¹ definition; 2×2 formula; invertibility iff columns are independent; elementary row operations (E₁,E₂,E₃) |
| 4 | Augmented matrices & representing systems | Writing Ax = b as [A|b]; linking matrix columns to basis images |

**Why here:** Matrices are the natural algebraic object once you know the vector space they act on (Day 2). Multiplication and inverses are the two operations you will reach for constantly in elimination (Day 5) and in numerical linear algebra (LAPACK dgesv, etc.).

---

## Day 4 — Determinants, Rank, and Singularity
**Main topic:** Scalar invariants that tell you whether a system is well-posed.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Determinant (2×2, 3×3 by cofactor expansion) | Geometric meaning (signed volume); det(AB)=det(A)det(B); det(Aᵀ)=det(A) |
| 2 | Rank of a matrix | rank = dim(col space) = dim(row space); how row ops change (or don't) rank |
| 3 | Singularity & invertibility criterion | A is singular ⇔ det A = 0 ⇔ rank < n ⇔ columns are dependent |
| 4 | Properties used in practice | det(kA)=kⁿdet(A); row/col swap flips sign; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged |

**Why here:** Determinant and rank are the "go/no-go" tests before solving. Knowing *whether* a unique solution exists (det≠0, full rank) prevents wasting time on a singular system. These invariants are also the basis of condition-number thinking in numerical linear algebra.

---

## Day 5 — Gaussian Elimination & Row Reduction
**Main topic:** The systematic algorithm for solving Ax = b.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Row echelon form (REF) & reduced row echelon form (RREF) | Pivots, free vs. pivot columns; uniqueness of RREF |
| 2 | Gaussian elimination (forward sweep) | Forward substitution after elimination; partial pivoting (swap rows for numerical stability — preview) |
| 3 | Gauss-Jordan elimination (full reduction) | Back-substitution absorbed into row ops; direct read-off of solution |
| 4 | Consistency & uniqueness via rank | rank(A)=rank([A|b]) → consistent; = n → unique; < n → infinitely many; inconsistent → no solution |

**Why here:** This is the core *procedure* that ties together vectors (columns), matrices (A, b), and the algebraic tests from Days 3–4. In numerical linear algebra, Gaussian elimination with pivoting **is** the basis of LAPACK's dgesv; understanding the hand algorithm first is essential.

---

## Day 6 — Solution Structure, Null Space, and Cramer's Rule
**Main topic:** What the *set* of solutions looks like, not just one solution.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Homogeneous (Ax=0) vs. inhomogeneous (Ax=b) systems | Particular solution + null-space component: x = xₚ + xₙ |
| 2 | Null space & column space (full treatment) | dim(null) + dim(col) = n (Rank-Nullity); basis for null space from free variables |
| 3 | Parametric (general) solution | Expressing all solutions with free parameters; geometric picture (line/plane in ℝⁿ) |
| 4 | Cramer's rule (n × n, det A ≠ 0) | xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A); useful for 2×2/3×3; computational cost O(n!) → motivates elimination |

**Why here:** Numerical linear algebra cares not just about *a* solution but about the *sensitivity* of the solution set (conditioning, perturbations). Understanding the null space and the particular+homogeneous decomposition is the prerequisite for that discussion.

---

## Day 7 — Review, Practice, and Synthesis
**Main topic:** Consolidate all six days; build pattern-recognition for technique selection.

| # | Sub-topic | Detail |
|---|-----------|--------|
| 1 | Mixed problem set (vectors → matrices → systems) | 15–20 problems spanning all topics; timed to simulate exam pressure |
| 2 | Technique-selection heuristics | When to use geometric (dot/cross) vs. algebraic (matrix) vs. algorithmic (elimination) approach |
| 3 | Common pitfalls & dimensional checks | Mismatched dimensions, forgetting det ≠ 0 before inverting, confusing row vs. column rank, arithmetic errors in elimination |
| 4 | Bridge to numerical linear algebra | Brief preview: floating-point round-off, partial vs. complete pivoting, why O(n³) elimination beats O(n!) Cramer, what condition number means (awareness only, no deep treatment) |

**Why here:** Spaced review at the end of the week cements the logical chain (vectors → spaces → matrices → invariants → algorithms → solution structure). The "bridge" sub-topic explicitly connects the hand-computed basics to the BLAS/LAPACK mindset expected in a numerical linear algebra course.

---

## Progression Logic (one-line summary)

Day 1 (what vectors *are*) → Day 2 (what spaces they *span*) → Day 3 (how matrices *represent* maps on those spaces) → Day 4 (scalar tests that *classify* a matrix) → Day 5 (the *algorithm* that solves a system) → Day 6 (the *structure* of the full solution set) → Day 7 (*synthesis* and bridge to numerical methods).

Each day's topics are a strict prerequisite for the next: you cannot form a matrix without vectors; you cannot test rank without independence; you cannot eliminate without knowing when the pivot matrix is invertible; you cannot interpret the solution set without understanding the null space.

parts.title: 7-Day Study Schedule
parts.body:
| Day | Main Topic | Sub-topics | Suggested Study Time | Suggested Practice / Exercise |
|-----|-----------|------------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
| 1 | Vectors in ℝ² and ℝ³ | Vector addition & scalar multiplication; dot product (inner product, projection); cross product (ℝ³); length, angle, unit vectors | 2–3 hrs | 6–8 component-wise arithmetic problems; compute dot & cross products, verify orthogonality, find unit vectors and angles between given vectors |
| 2 | Vector Spaces, Span & Linear Independence | Span & linear combinations; independence / dependence; basis & dimension; subspaces of ℝⁿ (row, column, null – intro) | 2–3 hrs | Determine span of 3–4 vector sets; prove / disprove independence; find a basis and dimension; sketch subspace geometry |
| 3 | Matrices & Matrix Operations | Addition, scalar mult., transpose; row-column multiplication (non-commutativity); inverse matrices & elementary row ops; augmented matrices for systems | 2–3 hrs | Multiply 2×3 · 3×2, 3×3 · 3×2; compute 2×2 inverses via formula; rewrite two linear systems as [A | b] augmented matrices |
| 4 | Determinants, Rank & Singularity | Cofactor expansion (2×2, 3×3); rank = dim(col/row space); singularity ⇔ det A = 0 ⇔ rank < n; key determinant properties | 2–3 hrs | Compute determinants of 2×2 and 3×3 matrices; find rank by row reduction; classify 6 given matrices as singular / non-singular with justification |
| 5 | Gaussian Elimination & Row Reduction | REF & RREF (pivots, free columns); Gaussian elimination (forward sweep + partial-pivoting preview); Gauss-Jordan (full reduction); consistency / uniqueness via rank | 2–3 hrs | Reduce four 3×3 and two 4×4 augmented matrices to RREF by hand; solve each system; state whether the solution is unique, infinite, or nonexistent |
| 6 | Solution Structure, Null Space & Cramer's Rule | Homogeneous vs inhomogeneous (x = xₚ + xₙ); null space & column space (Rank-Nullity); parametric general solution; Cramer's rule (n × n, det A ≠ 0) | 2–3 hrs | For three systems: find particular solution, basis for null space, write full parametric solution; verify Rank-Nullity; apply Cramer's rule to two 3×3 systems |
| 7 | Review, Practice & Synthesis | Mixed problem set (vectors → matrices → systems); technique-selection heuristics; common pitfalls & dimensional checks; bridge to numerical linear algebra (pivoting, O(n³) vs O(n!), condition number preview) | 3–4 hrs | 15–20 mixed problems (timed, ~45 min); self-diagnose weakest area; short written summary connecting elimination to LAPACK dgesv and the role of pivoting |

parts.title: Pre-NLA Concept Checklist
parts.body:
## Deliverable 2 — Pre-NLA Concept Checklist (10 items)

Tick each box only when you can explain *and* apply the concept without looking up notes.

1. **Vector norms (‖v‖₂, ‖A‖) and their role in measuring error**
   Every iterative solver, residual check, and convergence test in numerical linear algebra is expressed in terms of vector and matrix norms; without them you cannot quantify "how close" an approximate solution is to the exact one.

2. **Matrix multiplication as composition of linear maps, including non-commutativity and transpose rules**
   BLAS routines (DGEMM, DSYRK) and every factored solver build on row-column multiplication; knowing (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ, dimension compatibility, and AB ≠ BA in general lets you verify the correctness and efficiency of any composed algorithm.

3. **Determinant and its geometric / analytic meaning (signed volume, det(AB) = det A · det B)**
   det A = 0 is the single scalar test that flags a singular matrix, the threshold between a well-posed and an ill-posed linear system that every direct solver must detect before attempting a solve.

4. **Matrix inverse and the equivalent invertibility criteria (det ≠ 0, full rank, linearly independent columns)**
   Understanding A⁻¹ as a linear map (not merely a 2×2 formula) prepares you for the practical NLA insight that explicitly computing inverses is almost always replaced by factorisations to save both time and accuracy.

5. **Rank–Nullity theorem (dim null(A) + rank(A) = n) and construction of a null-space basis from free variables**
   Determines whether a homogeneous system has only the trivial solution and quantifies the degrees of freedom in under-determined or over-determined problems that NLA must handle via least-squares or regularisation.

6. **Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting (forward sweep to REF, then back-substitution)**
   This hand algorithm is the exact procedure behind LAPACK's DGETF2 / DGETRF and DGESV; executing it step-by-step builds the intuition for pivot growth, forward error, and the O(n³) cost model that underpins all dense direct solvers.

7. **LU triangular factorisation (A = LU) and its relationship to the elimination steps**
   Decomposing A into a lower and an upper triangular factor is the single most reused building block in dense NLA (repeated right-hand-side solves, rank updates, sensitivity analysis); recognising where LU hides inside your elimination work is the key conceptual leap.

8. **Condition number (intro: κ(A) = ‖A‖ · ‖A⁻¹‖) as a measure of solution sensitivity**
   Before running any numerical solve you must be able to state *whether* the problem is ill-conditioned; κ tells you roughly how many significant digits of b will be lost in x, which is the first question every NLA course asks.

9. **Orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace (via the dot-product / normal equations)**
   Least-squares solvers, QR factorisation, and Krylov-subspace iterative methods (GMRES, CG) all rest on projecting onto column spaces; the projection formula proj_w(v) = (v·w / w·w) w is the geometric seed from which those algorithms grow.

10. **System solvability and uniqueness via rank comparison (rank(A) vs. rank([A|b])**
    A numerical solver must first decide whether a solution exists and whether it is unique; these rank comparisons are the mathematical gate that every NLA routine implicitly performs, and mis-reading them leads to false convergence or missed inconsistency.
